picks.style: archaic greek fable-chant, single lyre and hand drum, storyteller's baritone, sparse, hard, unsettling
picks.why: The hawk carrying the nightingale in his talons and telling her why she should not cry out — the oldest fable in Greek, and it needs nothing around it.

picks.style: greek gnomic chant, plucked lyre over low drone, stern male voice, measured, climbing, austere
picks.why: 'Badness can be got easily and in shoals... but between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows' — the long steep path, the line the poem is remembered for.

picks.style: archaic greek hymn-proem, phorminx and drone, grave male voice, slow, invocatory, swelling
picks.why: The opening call to the Muses, with its hammering 'easily... easily... easily' — Zeus raising and levelling men, built as anaphora already.

picks.style: latin christian hymn, plainchant over organum drone, male schola, slow, luminous, awed
picks.why: 'I see the raging winds suddenly grow gentle... he himself walks over the flowing waves on shining soles' — an anaphoric catalogue of miracles that is already a hymn.

picks.style: late antique narrative chant, low male voices and struck bell, kindling, dramatic, fire-lit
picks.why: The furnace: three men thrown in, a fourth walking laughing through the flames, and the king's 'I confess it, and, vanquished, I adore.'

picks.style: latin funerary chant, deep unison voices and sparse drone, hollow, echoing, slow with a sudden call
picks.why: 'Come forth from the tomb, Lazarus, tell whose voice beneath the deepest earth you heard' — direct address to a dead man, and the gates of darkness opening.

picks.style: english broadside ballad, fiddle and side drum, mocking male voice, jaunty, brisk, jeering
picks.why: 'Come hither ye Dreamers of Dreams, ye Soothsayers, Vizards and Witches' — a proper street-ballad opening with a hook in the first line.

picks.style: georgian ballad of defiance, plain guitar and bass viol, weathered baritone, slow, unrepentant, plainspoken
picks.why: Defoe on his own muse: 'Satyr has been her Talent, Truth her Song... For this they've damn'd the Poet and his Rimes' — the pillory speaking.

picks.style: north-sea hymn, low strings and bodhran, granite bass voice, slow, immovable, storm-battered
picks.why: Sea-cliffs as the ocean's bridle and 'the Warts and Wrinkles plac'd on Natures Brow' — one sustained image, and it holds.

picks.style: english liberty ode, martial drum and trumpet, ringing baritone with chorus, driving trochaic pulse, defiant
picks.why: 'Let the stupid flock obey! Pent within a narrow fold, / Ty'd, and stript, and slain, and sold' — short lines, hard consonants, made for shouting.

picks.style: georgian pastoral ode, harpsichord and flute, genial tenor, flowing, sunlit, courtly
picks.why: The Lonsdale ode's landscape stanza — the crystal maze of the flood, the swan moving slow, the herds grazing on either side.

picks.style: georgian satirical air, plucked strings and light percussion, dry alto, clipped, epigrammatic, brisk
picks.why: 'Happy they whom crowds befriend, / Curs'd who on the crowd depend' — tight antithetical couplets that snap shut like a lid.

picks.style: georgian drawing-room song, harpsichord and violin, teasing soprano, lilting anapests, light, arch
picks.why: 'Prythee why so fantastick and vain! What charms can the toilet supply?' — a complete, funny, perfectly metrical lyric with a question in every stanza.

picks.style: anacreontic song, lute and light strings, warm storytelling tenor, brisk, candlelit, mischievous
picks.why: Cupid knocking at the door on a wet night, wings dripping, asking to be let in — the most charming small story in the book.

picks.style: english country dance tune, fiddle and tabor, bright chorus, jig time, foot-stamping, rustic
picks.why: The country wake with nimble Marian matchless in the jig and the lout winking at her blue stocking — pure dance-floor.

picks.style: scottish lament, fiddle and low drone, keening male voice, slow, mournful, strophic
picks.why: 'Mourn, hapless Caledonia, mourn thy banish'd peace, thy laurels torn' — Smollett's Culloden song, and a real refrain.

picks.style: highland elegy, clarsach and bodhran, grieving contralto, slow air, bleak, closing on the refrain
picks.why: The mother dying on the heath with her orphans crying for bread, and then the refrain returning to close the poem.

picks.style: english invocation-ode, chamber strings and lute, soft baritone, hushed, drowsy, lulling
picks.why: 'Soft Sleep, profoundly pleasing power... charm the canker Care away' — a clean short-lined invocation that could be a lullaby unaltered.

picks.style: english neoclassical recitation, solo harp over low drone, grave baritone, spacious, oracular, sparse
picks.why: Weak field, but this one holds real lines — 'Endure my heart' and Denham's 'strong without rage, without o'erflowing full' — and the sea questions close it.
